Reddit and Teladoc Shares Plummet, What You Need To Know
What Happened?

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 5% to levels not seen since 2007, lifting discount rates on long-duration growth earnings. According to CNBC, the 10-year yield surged to 5.23% on Friday, its highest level since 2007, after trading below 4.8% earlier in September. CNBC reported Monday that the yield was again pressing multiyear highs — above 5.23% in morning trade — as oil stayed elevated and investors braced for PCE, GDP, and jobs data. Macquarie strategist Thierry Wizman told CNBC the move reflects not only sticky inflation and Fed hike odds, but also heavy Treasury and corporate bond issuance, including AI-related borrowing. Higher yields raise borrowing costs and make distant cash flows look less attractive versus safer government bonds — a setup that tends to hit consumer-internet names such as DoorDash, Carvana, Reddit, Match, and Bumble harder than slower-growth sectors. Morningstar, citing Dow Jones, similarly said technology shares led early declines as the selloff in Treasuries extended into jobs week.

The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

Among others, the following stocks were impacted:

Zooming In On Reddit (RDDT)

Reddit's shares are extremely volatile and have had 60 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 18 days ago when the stock gained 6.7% on the news that Piper Sandler audience measurement data indicated that the platform's user base expanded 8% month-over-month in August 2026, marking its fastest monthly pace of the year. According to the research, the monthly acceleration pushed Reddit's year-over-year audience growth to 18.0%. The pickup in user traffic reflects expanding reach and stronger engagement across the social media platform. Investors closely monitor active user metrics as a key indicator of underlying business health and future advertising revenue potential, driving optimism around the company's growth trajectory.

A 39-year-old once owed more than they were worth after taking on six figures in student loans. Now, they're celebrating a $500,000 portfolio after watching years of slow progress suddenly pick up speed.

"Woohoo! Finally reached $500k milestone at 39!" they shared on Reddit.

They Had To Build Everything Without A Financial Head Start

The poster didn't come from money or receive an inheritance. Their family hadn't contributed toward tuition, rent, security deposits, furniture, moving expenses, appliances or other major expenses, leaving them to cover everything themselves from the beginning.

Someone who had paid off law school loans in their early 30s understood what it meant to start building wealth without that support.

"Family help really adds up and doesn't get factored in," the commenter said. "I remember paying off my law schools loans at 33/34 and finally being worth 0. It was a huge deal."

It Took 4.5 Years To Turn $100,000 Into $250,000

The original poster consistently contributed to a 401(k), Backdoor Roth IRA, Mega Backdoor Roth and health savings account. Still, going from $100,000 to $250,000 took about 4.5 years.

Then came a major job change with a big pay increase and large bonuses. The OP continued living the same way despite earning more.

"The difference in pay and all of the bonuses went directly to my retirement accounts," they said. "I kept the same lifestyle despite salary increases over the years."

A little under two years later, the portfolio had grown from $250,000 to $500,000.

The Student Loans Kept Them From Saving For A Down Payment

College had given the OP opportunities that eventually helped them earn more, but the debt came with a trade-off. Paying off the loans prevented them from saving for a down payment on a house.

They would make the same decision again. "If I could go back I would absolutely take the loans again. The long term return was worth the short term debt," the OP said, adding that the degree opened doors to opportunities, higher salaries and bonuses they otherwise wouldn't have had.

A 79-year-old retiree has been drawing from his retirement accounts for 14 years, yet he has more money today than when he stopped working at 65. That left his child wondering whether his own retirement could eventually play out the same way.

"Why are we all stressing so much about retirement?" he asked on Reddit.

His Father Has More Money Than When He Retired 14 Years Ago

The poster said his father's retirement accounts had grown despite his annual spending, with market growth appearing to outpace what he was taking from the portfolio.

That experience wasn't unusual to everyone. "Statistically, many/most people end up with more in their portfolios decades after retirement," a commenter wrote. "Also, most people spend less money in the later stages in life."

Spending habits came up as another reason. "I have read this occurs a good bit of the time as retirees can carry the frugality of their accumulative years into their retirement," someone else wrote.

Then there are expenses that can disappear or decline altogether. "Many retirees also no longer pay into a mortgage and have lower out of pocket healthcare costs on Medicare than they do with private healthcare," another person added.

His Retirement Date May Have Made All The Difference

The original poster's father retired after years that included the dot-com crash and the 2008 financial crisis, then spent much of the next 14 years invested as stock prices rose.

For some people, the timing said a lot. "Your father picked maybe the best time to retire, ever," someone wrote.

A 40-year-old father of two thought he still had more time before deciding whether to walk away from his career. Then he found out his employer was letting him go.

But with $3 million invested and his wife planning to keep working, he isn't looking for another job.

"I think I'm done!" he wrote on Reddit.

Forget The Rental Property. Some Investors Are Using Real Estate Notes Instead.

He Had $3 Million Invested And Still Planned To Work Longer

The poster had considered quitting eight months earlier but decided to work for at least another 18 months. At the time, they thought another three years on the job could put them in an even stronger position.

The poster's wife already had about $3 million invested in diversified stock exchange-traded funds, including roughly $700,000 in their 401(k)s. They had built most of their wealth through careers in law and tax advisory.

With the poster's wife planning to work for at least another three years, they don't need to start living off that money yet because her income covers their expenses.

"So basically I'm coast [financial independence, retire early]/ stay at home dad for now," they wrote.

Staying Home Means Taking On A Different Kind Of Work

The poster wants more time with their kids while they're young and more freedom to ski, mountain bike and occasionally take a midweek trip.

Someone who had been in a similar position suggested making home responsibilities part of their new routine. "Treat home stuff like a job," the person wrote, adding that they should "make sure she still gets time for her own activities."

There was also the day-to-day work of having two young children at home. "Might I suggest taking on the vast majority of household tasks like cooking, cleaning, groceries," one person wrote. "I have two kids under 4 years old and taking care of them is a full time job in itself…"

The $160,000 Question Comes Once They're Both Retired

Once they're both retired, the couple expects to spend about $160,000 a year, including taxes and health care. The original poster hopes their investments will be closer to $4 million by then and is comfortable starting with a withdrawal rate of about 5%.

title: Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028
detail:
Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028
Wiltone Asuncion
Sat, September 26, 2026 at 6:14 AM PDT 4 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Reddit Stock Is Down Nearly 35% in 2026, Yet Wall Street Sees Revenue Topping $5 Billion by 2028 ©@Brett Jordan from Pexels via Canva, @Karola G from Pexels via Canva
Key Stats for Reddit Stock

Current Price: $149.84

Target Price (Mid): ~$305

Street Target: ~$214

Potential Total Return: ~104%

Annualized IRR: ~18% / year

What Happened?

Reddit (RDDT) closed at $149.84 on September 25, down 34.8% from the end of 2025. Over the same stretch, TIKR consensus for 2028 revenue rose from around $4.8 billion to around $5.5 billion. That's past the range investors fear Reddit will stall in.

CEO Steve Huffman addressed that range at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on September 8, listing it among the misconceptions he hears: "I think investors worry that Reddit is going to get stuck at the $4 billion to $5 billion revenue range because some of our similarly scaled peers have gotten stuck there."

Huffman's Case Rests on Reach and Commerce

Huffman's case against the ceiling is reach and commerce: "our TAM is literally everybody," he said, and "40% of the conversations on Reddit are commercial."

Reddit has topped the high end of its own revenue guidance in each of the last five quarters, by 11% in Q2. Its Q3 guide of $860 million to $870 million implies growth of about 48% at the midpoint, down from 61% in Q2. The average estimate of around $872 million sits just above the top of that range.

Reddit Revenue & EBITDA (TIKR)
U.S. Users Explain Why Reddit Trades Below Meta

U.S. daily active uniques slipped to 53.2 million in Q2 from 53.5 million in Q1 as search referrals turned choppy. On July 30, Huffman said Google's AI Overviews can't replace traditional search links for traffic.

U.S. logged-in users grew just 1% year over year. U.S. revenue still grew 56%, as revenue per U.S. daily user rose 51% to $11.85. International daily users rose 28% to 77.1 million, with $2.26 in revenue each.

Shares fell 20.99% the session after the report. Reddit will also stop disclosing the logged-in split starting with Q3.

Huffman argued that traffic "that's logged out or transient is just less meaningful to us, which is why we can see volatility in SEO traffic, and that doesn't turn into volatility in our business."

Reddit's NTM P/E ratio of around 18x sits below Meta Platforms' at around 23x and Alphabet's at around 26x. The discount disappears on NTMEV/EBITDA, where Reddit's around 15x tops Meta's around 12x. The P/E flatters Reddit: its 2026 normalized EPS estimate of around $7.70 runs well above the GAAP estimate of around $5.40.

Reddit NTM Price / Normalized Earnings (P/E) (TIKR)

Reddit's content deals with Google and OpenAI reportedly expire next year. Huffman declined to discuss the Google talks in detail because Reddit is "in active negotiation." Other revenue, including licensing, was 5.3% of Q2 sales.
